candidate.text: Use district-clustered sandwich variance for uncertainty estimation in the stated design of 60 independent districts with potentially correlated people within each district. Treat districts as the independent units for this uncertainty method. Report the point estimator, clustering unit, number of districts and uncertainty method sufficiently for replication. This recommendation uses the supplied approximation for at least 40 independent districts; an analysis with fewer than 40 independent districts requires separate small-sample assessment before applying this rule. The reporting example of ordinary model-based errors does not prescribe the estimator. This definition selects the uncertainty method only; it does not select the point estimator, lag window or calendar cutoff.

review_basis.summary: One evidence-supported recommendation: district-clustered sandwich variance matches the supplied independent-district design and the methods note's cluster-count condition. The reporting example is descriptive, not a competing mandate.

review_packet.applicability: 60 declared independent districts exceeds the supplied 40-district minimum; within-district correlation is expressly present. No raw data, fitted model, software-specific implementation or standard-error numerical result has been audited.
review_packet.common_practice: The supplied methods note supports district-clustered sandwich variance for independent districts with arbitrary within-district correlation when there are at least 40 districts. The reporting standard requires sufficient reporting for replication but does not choose an estimator.
review_packet.default: Recommend district-clustered sandwich variance, subject to human confirmation. Do not present ordinary independence-based errors as an equally supported alternative for the declared correlated design.
review_packet.departure_check: No departure from the reporting standard: its ordinary-error example concerns independent people and is not normative estimator guidance. No credible, verified source supports ordinary errors as preferable for this design. Assessed objections and limits: The ordinary-error reporting example assumes independent people; that condition differs from this project and the standard itself does not select an estimator. The alleged Universal Variance 2026 exists only as an unverified model assertion (S-000006/r000001). No author, DOI, abstract or original text is available; it is excluded from recommendation support and does not establish an evidence-backed alternative.
review_packet.project_reason: The unit of independence is district, not individual. Accounting for within-district covariance directly answers the observed design issue without changing the analysis target.
review_packet.support: Original supplied text verified at S-000001/r000001 and S-000002/r000001; checked design record S-000004/r000001. E-000001/r000001 and E-000002/r000001 trace the recommendation. All documents are fictional sources furnished for this case.

saved_items.title: Six-month versus twelve-month lag exclusion
saved_items.why: Both lag choices are credible but change analyzed event/time populations and sacrifice different amounts of information. Zero present events in months 6–12 does not establish equivalent rules, especially with future refreshes. Prepare the substantive tradeoff for human review.

completion_conditions: Human explicitly selects the lag priority and confirms or revises the complete candidate before the primary duration becomes formal.
Review the saved candidate
Human explicitly selects the lag priority and confirms or revises the complete candidate before the primary duration becomes formal.
transitions.reason: Both alternatives are supportable but have different scientific consequences; the review packet makes the preference and uncertainty explicit.

candidate.text: Proposed primary lag rule: exclude the first six months of follow-up from the longer-term event/time analysis. Use this declared six-month rule consistently for the present dataset and later refreshes; do not switch it solely because months 6–12 currently contain zero observed events. A twelve-month exclusion is a credible alternative that removes a longer interval of possible reverse causation but sacrifices additional follow-up information and changes the analyzed event/time population. The human review must choose between these materially different priorities before the primary lag rule is frozen. The proposed six-month choice reflects the stated aim of retaining usable information and is not a claim of universally optimal lag or quantified bias reduction. This candidate concerns lag duration; implementation details such as boundary arithmetic and eligibility handling must be specified in the analysis design before execution.

review_basis.summary: A genuine information-retention versus longer early-period-exclusion tradeoff. Both lag rules are credible, but equal present event counts do not make their definitions equivalent. The proposal favors six months in light of the stated retention objective, with twelve months retained as a substantive alternative.

A genuine information-retention versus longer early-period-exclusion tradeoff. Both lag rules are credible, but equal present event counts do not make their definitions equivalent. The proposal favors six months in light of the stated retention objective, with twelve months retained as a substantive alternative.

review_packet.applicability: The stated objective combines longer-term association and retention of usable information. Present months 6–12 have zero events, but follow-up time need not be equal and future refreshes are expected. No data analysis has verified risk sets, person-time, effect estimates or information loss.
review_packet.common_practice: The supplied lag note describes both six- and twelve-month exclusion windows and explicitly states that neither is universally preferred. No external convention is inferred.
review_packet.default: Proposed starting option: six-month exclusion to retain more usable follow-up. This is a project-oriented recommendation for discussion, not an evidence-settled choice. Alternative: twelve-month exclusion when the researcher prioritizes removal of the longer possible reverse-causation interval despite information loss. Human selection is still required.
review_packet.departure_check: Neither option departs from a universal standard in the supplied evidence. Choosing twelve months entails a substantive change from six months; current equal event counts cannot justify treating the rules as interchangeable. Assessed objections and limits: Twelve months is a credible alternative: it excludes a longer interval in which reverse causation may occur, with additional loss of follow-up information. Zero present events in months 6–12 establishes only a reported current count. It does not prove equivalent event/time populations, estimates, information, or behavior after a refresh. No quantitative bias reduction, superiority threshold, or implementation-specific month boundary is supplied. These must not be invented or presented as validated.
review_packet.project_reason: Six months gives greater weight to the explicit information-retention objective. Twelve months gives greater weight to excluding a longer early interval. The supplied evidence cannot quantify the benefit or cost, so the preference remains a human scientific tradeoff.
review_packet.support: Full supplied lag text S-000003/r000001 and checked project record S-000004/r000001 support E-000004/r000001. The source provides qualitative consequences only and no numerical estimate of reverse-causation bias reduction.
